look_here_first: LOOK HERE FIRST · Western horsenettle has much BROADER, often DEEPLY LOBED green-to-gray-green leaves than silverleaf nightshade. It is a prickly or sometimes sparsely armed upright perennial, with large lavender/blue five-pointed flowers and a cluster of yellow anthers. Later it produces exposed smooth round GREEN-STRIPED young berries that turn YELLOW as they ripen—just like silverleaf, so yellow fruit or purple flowers ALONE cannot split them. Instead check the broad lobed leaf outline and measure ripe berry size (often ~2–3 cm on regional material), then compare silver-gray felt on a typical silverleaf nightshade.

key_traits.label: Family pattern
key_traits.text: Solanaceae/Solanum: alternate leaves, 5-parted rotate or star-shaped corollas, poricidal anthers, and berry fruits; prickles and stellate hairs occur in many species.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: upright perennial herb to about 0.8–1 m, often stout and erect

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: ALTERNATE simple, ovate broadly outlined leaves with 2–4 irregular lobes per side (sometimes shallower); typically 5–16 x 2.5–10 cm

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: surface often GREEN to gray-green, stellate hairy but lacks typical dense SILVER FELT of silverleaf nightshade

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: stems, petioles and leaf veins may carry scattered cream/yellowish straight sharp prickles, sometimes sparse or absent

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: lavender, bluish purple or occasionally white 5-lobed star/rotate flowers commonly 2–4.6 cm across

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: five clustered YELLOW anthers, subequal in length; pale style may project beyond them

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: young green berries can display darker stripes like silverleaf nightshade

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: exposed round yellow ripe berries, generally larger than silverleaf: botanical revision 1.3–2.5 cm wide; UT Williamson county specimens ~2.5–3 cm

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: calyx mostly a small spreading/reflexed collar under ripe berry, not a prickly enclosure like buffalobur

key_traits.label: Habit
key_traits.text: Perennial erect herb, often coarse and 0.4–1 m tall. Stems one to a few from base with branching near upper plant; moderately star-hairy. Do not assume a rhizome is proven from an aboveground photograph.

key_traits.label: Leaf
key_traits.text: Alternate simple leaves. Mature blades are usually broad OVATE, sometimes asymmetric at base, with strongly or weakly sinuate/lobed margins and 2–4 main side lobes per edge. Flora of North America gives blade 6–15 × 3–10 cm; UT Williamson County treatment documents leaves occasionally up to 20 × 13 cm. Surfaces stellate-hairy but not usually uniformly silver-white like silverleaf nightshade.

key_traits.label: Prickles
key_traits.text: Cream to yellow, straight or slightly curved, often spaced on round stems, petioles and occasionally larger leaf veins, sometimes absent or sparse; lengths up to ~6.5 mm on stems in FNA. These are surface prickles, not branched woody thorns.

key_traits.label: Flower
key_traits.text: Typically a five-rayed lavender-to-blue-violet or occasionally white fused corolla roughly 2–4.6 cm across. Five bright yellow somewhat grouped anthers are generally SUBEQUAL, 5–9 mm, and open by small pores at distal tips. A pale style extends from their center with greenish stigma. Flowers in extra-axillary branched inflorescences.

lookalikes.differences: Broader greener leaves and larger overall build than silverleaf nightshade; much less densely prickly than buffalobur.
